key_insight: The paper shows how to let an LLM write and run native ARTIQ control code on trapped-ion hardware while enforcing a strict authorization boundary for every hardware-affecting operation.
engineering_relevance: It provides a practical safety architecture for autonomous quantum labs, enabling agent-driven calibration and control without giving unchecked software direct access to fragile experimental equipment.
method: LLM agent uses ARTIQ through a Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool layer.
Every tool call must carry an authorization token bound to the exact command contents.
Tokens are issued either by simulation-based validation against device bounds (dax.sim) or by a human for sensitive actions.
evidence_signal: The system was deployed on a co-trapped 40Ca+/40CaOH+ platform for autonomous calibration and cross-instrument magnetic-field stabilization, and portability was confirmed on an independent 171Yb+ platform.
watch_item: The protection boundary is only as strong as the tokening and simulation checks, so adversarial bypass attempts and unmodeled hardware behavior remain important risks.
paper_title: A hardware-safety-gated system for LLM-written native ARTIQ control code on a trapped-ion platform
